title: Notice Walk Detective
intro: Look around a Michigan backyard. Tap each thing you notice and watch your tally grow. Then pick the questions we can test and the ones we cannot.
note: This is a model of a real notice walk. Go outside or look around your room and notice real things too, then do the paper-towel test from the lesson. Do it with a grown-up.
summary: Noticing and asking are science, and your tally is data: 4 smooth things and 5 bumpy things, 5 from nature and 4 made by people. A question we can test changes one thing and measures one thing, like the towel test: Towel A held 5 drops, Towel B held 8 drops. A fair test keeps everything else the same, and opinions and big "why" questions are not tests yet.

items.say: A stone from the lake shore. Smooth! It is from nature.

items.say: A glass marble. Smooth! People made it.

items.label: Maple leaf
items.say: A maple leaf. Smooth! It is from a tree.

items.label: Pine cone
items.say: A pine cone. Bumpy! It is from a tree.

items.label: Tree bark
items.say: Tree bark. Bumpy! It is from a tree.

items.label: Acorn cap

items.label: Kitchen sponge

items.label: Old brick

choices.label: Which paper towel holds more drops of water?
choices.why: Yes! Change one thing: the towel. Measure one thing: the drops. The lesson did this: Towel A held 5 drops, Towel B held 8 drops.

choices.label: Why is water wet?
choices.why: A test changes one thing and measures one thing. This question has nothing to change or count yet.

choices.label: Is blue the prettiest color?
choices.why: Prettiest is an opinion. A test measures something we can count or compare.

questions.q: Look at your tally of smooth and bumpy things. Which question can we test?

choices.label: Does a marble roll farther on smooth paper or on a bumpy brick?
choices.why: Yes! Change one thing: the surface. Measure one thing: how far the marble rolls. Keep the same marble and the same push.

choices.label: Which is the nicest bumpy thing?
choices.why: Nicest is an opinion. A test measures something we can count or compare.

choices.label: Why did we find more bumpy things than smooth things?
choices.why: We just picked what was in the yard. There is nothing to change and measure, so this is not a test.

choices.label: Which ball rolls farther: on grass or on the sidewalk?
choices.why: Yes! Change one thing: the ground. Measure one thing: how far the ball rolls.

choices.label: Why is the sky blue?
choices.why: A test changes one thing and measures one thing. We cannot change the sky or count it here yet.

choices.label: What is the best backyard?
choices.why: Best is an opinion. A test measures something we can count or compare.

choices.label: Which soaks up more water: a sponge or a paper towel?
choices.why: Yes! Change one thing: what soaks up the water. Measure one thing: how much water it holds.

choices.label: Why do leaves fall off trees?
choices.why: A test changes one thing and measures one thing. This question has nothing we can change and count yet.

choices.label: Are pine cones nicer than stones?
choices.why: Nicer is an opinion. A test measures something we can count or compare.

questions.q: Which question is a fair test of paper towels?

choices.label: Which of two same-size towels holds more drops from the same dropper?
choices.why: Yes! Only the towel changes. The size and the dropper stay the same, so the towel is the only thing that can explain a different count.

choices.label: Does a big towel with big drops hold more than a small towel with small drops?
choices.why: That changes two things at once, the towel size and the drop size. If the counts differ, we could not tell which one did it. A fair test changes one thing and keeps the rest the same.

choices.label: Which towel do we like best?
choices.why: Liking is an opinion. A test measures something we can count or compare.
